en: I take refuge in that state of Rāma, which the sages attain through the awakening born of a purified mind via the sacrifice of the body— the Prāṇāgnihotra Upaniṣad.
Oṃ. May He protect us both together; may He nourish us both together; may we work together with great vigor;
may our study be brilliant; may we never harbor mutual hatred.
Oṃ, peace, peace, peace!
Hariḥ Oṃ.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the sacrifice of the body (*śārīrayajña*), which is the essence of all Upaniṣads, a hymn of mantras that transcends the knowledge of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*). It is that within which a person dwells in this very body, even without the fire-sacrifice (*agnihotra*) and even without Sāṃkhya-Yoga.

"Liberation from *saṃsāra* occurs. Having placed the food on the ground according to his own ritual rule, he consecrates it with the three verses beginning "The herbs whose king is Soma" and with the two verses beginning "O Lord of Food. "The many herbs whose king is Soma, which are of a hundredfold appearance..."
Impelled by Bṛhaspati, may they release us from sin. || 1 ||
Those plants which bear fruit and those which are fruitless, those which are without flowers and those which are flowering— impelled by Bṛhaspati, may they release us from distress.
O Mother of the living, who art never to be harmed, we bind this medicinal herb;
may it carry away the life of the enemy and drive away the demons. 3.
O Lord of Food, grant us food that is free from disease and full of vigor;
further the giver, and bestow strength upon our bipeds and quadrupeds. 4.
Whatever food has been consumed in various ways by Agni, or devoured by the Rudras or by the Piśācas—
may Īśāna render all of that free from danger.
To Śiva Īśāna, svāhā! || 5 ||
You move within all beings, dwelling in their secret cave, facing every direction.
You are the sacrifice; you are Brahmā; you are Rudra; you are Viṣṇu; you are the *vaṣaṭ* call;
you are water, light, essence, immortality, Brahman, *bhūr*, *bhuvaḥ*, *suvar*, and *oṃ*. Salutations!

May the waters purify the earth; may the purified earth purify me. May Brahmaṇaspati purify [me]; may that which is purified by the Veda purify me. Whatever is left over, whatever is unfit to be eaten, or whatever evil deed has been committed by me—[may all that be purified].
May the waters purify me from all acceptance of what is unrighteous, svāhā!
You are nectar; you are the under-layer for nectar. I offer nectar into the vital breath. You are the end of the blessing.
Svāhā to the out-breath! Svāhā to the in-breath! Svāhā to the diffused breath! Svāhā to the upward breath!

"To Samāna, svāhā!"—with these words, he offers into the *prāṇa* with the little finger and the thumb; into the *apāna* with the ring finger; into the *vyāna* with the middle finger; into the *udāna* with all the fingers; and into the *samāna* with the index finger. He makes one silent offering into the *ekarṣi*; two into the *āhavanīya*.
One [oblation] in the Dakṣiṇāgni fire; one in the Gārhapatya fire; and one in the Sarvaprāyaścittīya fire.
Then, having touched the lid for the sake of immortality, and taking it up again, he should touch it once more.
Having taken those waters which are your vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and having touched his heart, he should mutter:
"The vital breath is Agni, the Supreme Self, enveloped by the five winds."
I grant fearlessness to all beings; I have no fear at any time.
Thus ends the first section. || 1 ||
You are the All, the Vaiśvānara; the universe in its being born is sustained by you. You are the All, the oblation, and the whole where Brahman is immortal—you are this great Person.
"He who is established on the tip of the thumb—him I sprinkle with waters, that he may be for immortality at the end of this life. This external self, being unaging, should meditate:
'I offer the Agnihotra. He becomes the son of all."
He offers oblations surrounded by this sacrifice, thinking, "I am transforming the sacrifice within my own body. What is the portion of those four fires?
Therein, the fire named Sūrya has the form of the solar disc and possesses a thousand rays.

Surrounded by these, one becomes a single seer (*ṛṣi*) and stands at the head; because it is called the "fire of vision" (*darśanāgni*), it has four forms and, having become the *āhavanīya* fire, stands in the mouth.
The fire named "bodily" (*śārīra-agni*), which dispels old age, leaps upon the oblation; its form is that of a half-moon.
Having become the *dakṣiṇāgni*, it abides in the heart; therein is what is called the *koṣṭhāgni*.
Having properly cooked what is eaten, drunk, licked, and chewed through its individual functions, the *koṣṭhāgni* becomes the *gārhapatya* and abides in the navel.
Below that, there are three horizontal layers with the luster of moonlight;
their function is procreation.
Thus ends the second section. || 2 ||
In this sacrifice of the body, which is adorned with the sacrificial post and its rope, who is the sacrificer? Who is the wife? Who are the officiating priests? Who are the members of the assembly?
What are the sacrificial vessels? What are the oblations? What is the altar?
What is the *kottaravedi*? What is the *droṇakalaśa*? What is the chariot? What is the sacrificial animal?
Who is the *adhvaryu*? Who is the *hotṛ*? Who is the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin*? Who is the *pratiprasthātṛ*? Who is the *prastotṛ*? Who is the *maitrāvaruṇa*?

Who is the Udgātṛ? Who is the Dhārāpotr? What are the darbha grasses? What is the sruva ladle? What is the ājya-sthālī vessel? What are the two āghāra libations? What are the two ājyabhāga portions? What here are the yājyās? What are the anuyājās? What is the iḍā? What is the sūktavāka?
What is the word for well-being? What is violence? What are the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings?
What is the sacrificial post? What is the cord? What are the sacrifices? What is the sacrificial fee? What is the purificatory bath?
Thus ends the third section. || 3 ||
In this sacrifice of the body, which is adorned with the sacrificial post and its cord, the Self is the sacrificer;

the intellect is the wife; the Vedas are the great officiating priests; the ego is the Adhvaryu priest; the mind is the Hotṛ priest; the out-breath is the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin priest; and the down-breath is the Pratiprasthātṛ priest.

The *vyāna* breath is the *prastotṛ*; the *udāna* breath is the *udgātṛ*; the *samāna* breath is the *maitrāvaruṇa*. The body is the altar (*vedi*); the nose is the high altar (*uttaravedi*); the head is the *droṇakalaśa* vessel; the feet are the chariot; the right hand is the *sruva* ladle; and the left hand is the butter-pot (*ājyasthālī*).
The two Āghāra libations are the ears; the two Ājyabhāga portions are the eyes; the Dhruvā and Pota ladles are the neck;

the subtle elements (tanmātras) are the Sadasyas; the great elements (mahābhūtas) are the Prayājas; the gross elements and their qualities are the Anuyājas; the tongue is the Iḍā; the teeth and lips are the Sūktavāka; and the palate is...
The words of auspiciousness are the *śaṃyuvāka* hymns; mindfulness, compassion, patience, and non-violence are the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings;

the syllable *oṃ* is the sacrificial post (*yūpa*); hope is the tethering rope (*raśanā*); the mind is the chariot; desire is the sacrificial animal (*paśu*); the hair is the *darbha* grass; the organs of perception are the sacrificial vessels; and the organs of action [are the implements].

The oblations are non-violence; the sacrifices are self-restraint; the sacrificial fee is renunciation; and the final purificatory bath is death. For all the deities are indeed established within this body.
Whether one dies in Vārāṇasī or recites this [text] which is Brahman, by means of that single [act], one attains liberation.
"By birth alone a living being may attain liberation"—thus [ends] the Upaniṣad. 3.
Oṃ. May He protect us both together; may He nourish us both together; may we work together with great vigor.
May our study be radiant; may we never harbor mutual enmity.
Oṃ. Peace, peace, peace.
Hariḥ Oṃ Tat Sat.
Thus ends the Prāṇāgnihotra Upaniṣad.
